newsitem.title: USA: Key House lawmaker reoffers open power market bill.
newsitem.headline: Key House lawmaker reoffers open power market bill.

text.p: A key U.S. House lawmaker Monday reintroduced a sweeping bill to make states open their electricity markets to competition before 2001.

The bill by Republican Rep. Dan Schaefer of Colorado, chairman of the House energy and power subcommittee, would require states to clear the way for all consumers to be able to choose their own power suppliers by December 15, 2000, as in last year's proposal, his spokeswoman said.
In contrast, a similar bill introduced 10 days ago by Sen. Dale Bumpers, a Democrat from Arkansas, set the deadline for opening markets at the end of 2003.

All power producers would have to have credits either by generating power from biomass, landfill gas, wind, solar or geothermal energy, or by purchasing credits from power producers who do use those renewable energy sources.
A spokeswoman for Schaefer said the bill included some minor changes from last year, but details on the changes were not immediately available.
Schaefer and House Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, have said restructuring the electricity market is one of their top priorities this year.

Other House lawmakers have said they would reintroduce bills they offered last year, including proposals to link power market changes to tighter clean air standards and give states leeway to decide whether to deregulate power markets.
The main missing piece in the debate now is a long-awaited proposal from the Clinton administration.

The Energy Department, which is leading the effort to outline the administration's views, does not favor imposing a deadline on states to open their markets and wants to let states decide to how much utilities should be allowed to recoup from customers potential losses on assets they were required to build or buy in the regulated market.

But department officials have said the proposal could change as it is reviewed by several other agencies, including the Defense Department, which is a major electricity consumer, and the Agriculture Department, which has $33 billion in loans outstanding to rural utilities.
